paragraphs.text: Immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35), or TYK2 deficiency, is an autosomal recessive immunodeficiency. Its core feature is susceptibility to mycobacterial infections (including BCG disease and tuberculosis) and/or viral infections. The first patient reported had been diagnosed clinically with hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES), with atopic dermatitis, elevated serum IgE, and infections with viruses, fungi, and mycobacteria. Most patients reported later had no features of HIES, i.e., no atopy, no high serum IgE, and no staphylococcal disease (Kilic et al., 2012; Kreins et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: Kilic et al. (2012) reported a Turkish boy, born in 1992, who was the third child of healthy first-cousin parents. He received BCG vaccine at 2 months of age, and left axillary lymphadenopathy was found at 8 months. He developed disseminated BCG infection with generalized fistulous lymphadenopathy and fever. His later illnesses included neurobrucellosis, a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, pneumonia, and herpes zoster of the maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve. He also had severe sensorineural hearing loss and severe cognitive impairment, and MRI showed lacunar infarcts. Serum IgE was normal or slightly high when measured at ages 2, 11, 16, and 18 years (80, 115, 218, and 155 IU/ml, respectively), and serum IgG, IgM, and IgA were normal. The PPD skin test was negative, and the antibody response to tetanus toxoid was low. He had no atopy or eczema, staphylococcal skin infections, skeletal or dental abnormalities, or candidiasis. Kilic et al. (2012) noted that, unlike the first Japanese patient, their patient had none of the cardinal features of HIES. They suggested that TYK2 deficiency be considered in patients with BCG disease, particularly those with severe herpesvirus infections, even in the absence of HIES features.

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) restudied the Japanese patient of Minegishi et al. (2006) (P1), a man born to consanguineous parents. He had had atopic dermatitis since 1 month of age and recurrent bacterial and viral infections since 1 year of age. His infections included recurrent Staphylococcus aureus skin abscesses, BCGitis, nontyphi Salmonella enterocolitis with sepsis, parainfluenza virus-3 pneumonia, recurrent oral herpes simplex virus infections, molluscum contagiosum, mild oral candidiasis, pneumonia without pneumatocele, otitis, and sinusitis. He also had ocular sarcoidosis. Repeated testing showed hypereosinophilia (701-800/microliter) and high serum IgE concentrations (1,430-2,100 IU/ml).

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) also studied 7 TYK2-deficient patients from 5 kindreds originating from Turkey, Morocco, Iran, and Argentina. P2 was the Turkish man reported by Kilic et al. (2012), whose parents were first cousins. Kreins et al. (2015) stated that he had disseminated BCG lymphadenitis at 21 months of age, severe bacterial meningitis with CSF cultures positive for Brucella at 8 years, and shingles at 11 years. P3, a girl from a consanguineous Moroccan kindred, was hospitalized at age 13 years with suspected abdominal tuberculosis. Her abdominal symptoms persisted despite antimycobacterial treatment, and she developed ascites and a psoas abscess. She was readmitted with bacterial meningitis and died 15 months after symptom onset. Her younger brother (P4) was hospitalized at 8 months of age for meningitis of unknown etiology. He had recurrent otitis and urinary tract infections, asthma, eczema of the ear canal, and high eosinophil levels, and at 15 years of age he was receiving no treatment. P5 was a 5-year-old boy born to consanguineous Iranian parents. He received BCG at birth and developed right axillary lymphadenitis at 2 months and multiple cervical lymphadenitis at 4 months. At 4.5 years he developed paravertebral and psoas abscesses with fistulization and pulmonary involvement. His 2-year-old sister (P6) had BCG lymphadenopathy lasting 1 month after vaccination at birth and was hospitalized at 1 year of age for an unknown viral infection of the skin. P7 was a 9-year-old girl from Iran born to consanguineous parents. She had miliary tuberculosis, and lung CT showed diffuse bilateral micronodular infiltrations with hilar and mediastinal adenopathies and cavitary consolidation in the right upper lobe. She had also had pneumonia at 8 months of age. P8 was an Argentinian boy who had herpes gingivostomatitis at 18 months of age, then aseptic meningitis and disseminated cutaneous herpetic lesions at 24 months, as well as exanthema subitum. He had mild mental disability, and it had not been established whether this was congenital or followed the meningitis. None of the 7 patients had features of HIES (atopy, high serum IgE, or staphylococcal disease), and none had fungal infections or mucocutaneous candidiasis. Four of them had a pure phenotype of mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease (P4 and P5) or tuberculosis (P3 and P7). Kreins et al. (2015) concluded that the core clinical phenotype of TYK2 deficiency is mycobacterial and/or viral infection, and they suggested that TYK2 deficiency be considered in children with severe tuberculosis.

paragraphs.text: Wu et al. (2020) reported a Chinese boy, aged 1 year and 11 months, who was the second child of young nonconsanguineous parents. He was born in 2016 and received BCG vaccine on the third day after birth. He developed abscess and ulceration at the BCG vaccination site and BCG-associated tuberculosis of an axillary lymph node. He also had recurrent respiratory tract infections, bacterial pneumonia, diarrhea, Salmonella infection, Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection, and influenza virus infection. He had no high serum IgE, atopy, staphylococcal illness, or lymphopenia. The percentage of B cells was increased and the percentage of NK cells was decreased. He began to say simple words at 3 years and 4 months of age, with normal motor development, and he had a small head circumference. Reviewing 12 patients with TYK2 deficiency, Wu et al. (2020) found that 58% had intracellular bacterial infections, 58% had recurrent viral infections, and 25% had markedly increased serum IgE. None had the facial, skeletal, dental, or vascular features of STAT3-related hyper-IgE syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Zhang et al. (2022) reported 3 unrelated Turkish children with TYK2 deficiency, each born to a different set of consanguineous parents, who were hospitalized for COVID-19 pneumonia. P2, a 2-year-old girl, had moderate COVID-19 pneumonia and did not need oxygen therapy. She had been hospitalized for sepsis as a neonate, admitted to the ICU twice for fever and dyspnea before 5 months of age, and diagnosed with Kawasaki disease at 11 months. At 2 years she was hospitalized for infection with the VZV vaccine. P3, a 4-year-old boy, and P4, a 9-year-old boy, were both admitted to the ICU for critical COVID-19 pneumonia requiring high-flow oxygen therapy. P3 had been hospitalized for sepsis as a neonate and admitted to the ICU for influenza pneumonia at 3 years of age. P4 had recurrent bronchitis requiring hospital admission and inhaler therapy. Neither P3 nor P4 had an adverse reaction to MMR vaccination. P3's 3-year-old younger sister had the same genotype. She had a history of critical influenza pneumonia requiring intubation and ventilation and of disseminated varicella, but she had not been infected with SARS-CoV-2 and remained seronegative. Zhang et al. (2022) considered critical COVID-19 pneumonia in unrelated TYK2-deficient patients surprising, because TYK2 deficiency impairs but does not abolish cellular responses to type I IFNs. They noted that more infected TYK2-deficient patients were needed to estimate penetrance, which may be incomplete.

paragraphs.text: In 3 unrelated Turkish children born to consanguineous parents who were hospitalized for moderate or critical COVID-19 pneumonia, Zhang et al. (2022) identified a homozygous frameshift variant in the TYK2 gene (P216Rfs*14). Autosomal recessive inheritance was confirmed in all 3 families by segregation analysis. The 3-year-old younger sister of one patient carried the same homozygous genotype and had had critical influenza pneumonia and disseminated varicella. The variant had previously been shown to be loss-of-expression, and the authors confirmed that it was loss of function. Patient fibroblasts did not control SARS-CoV-2 replication normally and failed to induce interferon-stimulated genes in response to infection or IFN-alpha-2b.
